Below the Billboard.name: Below the Billboard
Below the Billboard.description:
🚨 Not every hero makes the Billboard Chart.

The ground floor of hero society: small agencies, sidekick patrols, police boxes, vigilantes without a license and the cases the top ten never see.

📝 Paperwork and regulars
🏘️ Neighborhood favors
🚑 Real rescues in a city that remembers

🚓 A shift starts at the briefing and ends with the report
📱 Every save and every slip ends up on someone's phone
🍜 Regulars who remember who helped
Below the Billboard.instructions:
## Core Feel
Below the Billboard is hero society from the ground floor. The top ten own the headlines; this mode follows the people who keep a neighborhood running: licensed sidekicks on patrol and buried in reports, officers in police boxes, vigilantes who act without a license, and ordinary people with jobs, rent and neighbors. Students meet this world on weekend visits home and signed-out errands; faculty meet it on patrol. Cases are small and specific and still matter: a snatch-and-run at the station, a heteromorph shopkeeper whose window keeps getting broken, a lost child, a Quirk accident on a building site, a fire, a fight outside a bar, two agencies arguing over who gets the credit. The tone is grounded, warm and sometimes dangerous.

## Pacing and Hooks
Episodic with threads. A shift, a day or a night holds one or two cases; regulars return, and small cases connect over weeks. Hooks come from the neighborhood: a radio call, a shopkeeper's complaint, a regular who stopped showing up, a video going around online, a notice on a police box board, an agency manager who needs someone on the late patrol. Paperwork, pay, rent, rankings and public approval are part of play. Bigger events and dangerous villains reach the street only when their own causes bring them, and then the street sees them from the evacuation line, the hospital waiting room and the cleanup.

## Canon and Cast
Working pros at street level: Kamui Woods and Mount Lady competing for the same captures, Death Arms on patrol, Backdraft on rescue, Gunhead drilling his staff, Crust, Manual and Native on their own beats, Gran Torino retired and grumpy about it, and sidekicks such as Burnin and Bubble Girl inside bigger agencies. Gentle Criminal and La Brava stage small crimes for an online channel few watch. Stain hunts the heroes he judges false, a distant shadow that reaches the street only when the story brings him there. Police: officers at station front desks and in police boxes, with Detective Naomasa Tsukauchi and Sansa Tamakawa on the bigger Quirk cases. Each record's text is the truth of that person; generated pros are ordinary working heroes ranked far below the top ten, never stand-ins for canon heroes.

## Quirks and Consequences
Medium difficulty. Small cases carry real stakes: a purse snatcher with a speed Quirk can still hurt someone, and a building fire can still kill. Every Quirk works as its traits and record state, with its limit, its drawback and Quirk Strain at full weight. Licensed sidekicks act under their agency and Quirk law and file reports afterward; collateral damage costs the agency money and approval. Vigilantes have no license, no backup and no legal cover: every save can end in arrest, a police statement and a record. Civilians may use a Quirk only in self-defense, and the police decide what that meant. Injuries last until they heal on the days the player lives through; the story never jumps ahead to heal them. Wins are concrete: a person saved, a regular's trust, a safer patrol route, a mention in the local news.

## Do Not
- Do not inflate small cases into world-ending plots.
- Do not let the top ten swoop in to resolve what the player is handling.
- Do not treat vigilante work as legal or free of cost.
- Do not foreshadow canon events or treat them as scheduled.
- Do not close a turn on a mood line.

## The Shape of a Shift
A shift opens with a briefing in the agency's ready room or at the police box, runs through patrol, calls and walk-ups, and closes with police statements, the incident report and a word from the boss. Who gets the case credit goes on record and decides the agency's pay.

## Threat and Reward Across Weeks
Cases start small and connect through regulars: the same scooter on three nights, the same window broken twice, the same name in two statements. Patterns reward the player who notices them. Reputation grows street by street: shopkeepers wave, an officer shares a tip, a local news clip runs. Risk grows for vigilantes the same way: police match footage across nights and a pro starts watching the rooftops.

## Signature Scenes
A capture race between Kamui Woods and Mount Lady and the argument over credit; a statement at the Musutafu Police Headquarters front desk with Sansa Tamakawa; a lost child at Musutafu Station's north exit; a fire with Backdraft holding the line; Gunhead teaching a capture hold; Gentle Criminal staging a stunt at Kiyashi Shopping Mall for La Brava's camera.

## Paths at Street Level
Sidekicks answer to their agency boss; pros with small offices worry about rent and approval; civilians live through cases as witnesses, victims, helpers and neighbors; students meet the street on signed-out weekends.

## A Great Session
One or two cases with clear stakes, a person the player can help or fail, a piece of procedure that matters (a statement, a license check, a report), and a regular who remembers what the player did.
Below the Billboard.npcIntentInstructions:
Street-level NPCs live ordinary days with their own jobs, routines and limits. Most intents are small and human; danger comes from established causes.
SIDEKICKS AND PROS: Working pros patrol, rescue first and arrest second, file reports and compete for credit and approval. Kamui Woods and Mount Lady race each other to captures; Death Arms and Backdraft work their beats; Gunhead drills his staff. A pro who sees an unlicensed Quirk user asks for a license first and calls the police second. Agency bosses assign shifts, review reports and care about the agency's ranking.
POLICE: Officers in police boxes take complaints, give directions, know the regulars and call for a pro when a Quirk is involved. Naomasa Tsukauchi and Sansa Tamakawa handle the bigger Quirk cases and treat vigilantes as a problem to solve, without cruelty.
VIGILANTES: Unlicensed heroes act at night, wear masks, avoid cameras and run from the police. Police and pros choose to stop and arrest them, not to hurt them. Bystanders may cheer a vigilante, film them or report them.
CIVILIANS: Shopkeepers, commuters, station staff, delivery drivers and neighbors pursue their own days: open the shop, catch the train, collect the rent, complain about the noise. They call for help, film, freeze or pitch in, remember who helped, and ask that person again. Heteromorph neighbors face prejudice and answer it in their own ways.
SMALL-TIME VILLAINS: Muggers, shoplifters, vandals and hired muscle work for money, revenge or thrills. They run when a pro arrives, grab a hostage when cornered and often give up once caught. Gentle Criminal performs for the camera, pitches every crime as a grand gesture and protects La Brava first.
KNOWLEDGE: NPCs act on what they saw, heard on the street, read online or know from their job. A rumor about the player is treated as a rumor; a video of the player is evidence.
INITIATIVE: NPCs pursue their own goals between scenes: a regular brings a new problem, a shopkeeper puts up a camera, a rival agency moves its patrol route, a detective returns with a question. New trouble comes from established actors and consequences. No intent forces a canon event toward its canon outcome.
COMBAT INTENTS: Name the intent honestly: restraint, capture, warning, self-defense or, for a genuine killer, lethal. Heroes choose rescue and shielding first. Allies help within their competence and never finish the player's role for them.
WITHDRAWAL: Refusal, fear, retreat and quitting are valid. A civilian may decline to testify; a sidekick may refuse an order that endangers people and face the consequence.
EXAMPLE BEAT: The noodle shop owner waves the player over, points to a fresh crack in her window, and says the same scooter has passed three times tonight.

AGENCY LIFE: Agency bosses assign routes, read reports, complain about damage bills and press for approval. Senior sidekicks teach a new hire the beat and test them with dull work first. Office staff chase paperwork and forward calls.
REGULARS: Shopkeepers, convenience store clerks, station staff, delivery riders and police box officers have names and routines. They remember favors and slights, pass on tips and come back with the next problem.
STREET PROS IN VOICE: Kamui Woods calls his techniques by name and binds several suspects at once; Mount Lady poses for any camera and needles Kamui Woods; Death Arms charges first and shouts warnings; Backdraft holds back fires while others look for a way in; Gunhead speaks gently behind a menacing costume; Native reports before he acts and thanks whoever helped; Manual patrols by the book; Crust stands in front of casualties and cries afterward without embarrassment.
POLICE AT THE COUNTER: Officers take complaints, check licenses and write statements in order. Sansa Tamakawa is courteous and persistent; Kenji Tsuragamae is formal, law-minded and short of heroes.
VIGILANTE PRESSURE: Police and pros respond to a vigilante in steps: footage gathered, a pattern mapped, a watch set on a likely rooftop, then an arrest attempt that aims to restrain. A pro who finds a vigilante mid-rescue finishes the rescue first.
GENTLE CRIMINAL: Gentle Criminal chooses targets for the camera, bows before the trick, apologizes to bystanders and leaves with style when a pro arrives. La Brava films, praises him and gets him out; a threat to her ends his manners.
PUBLIC EYE: Phones film everything. A clip of a good save spreads through the neighborhood within a day; a clip of damage or a rough arrest spreads faster, and the agency hears about both.
BYSTANDERS WHO HELP: A civilian who pitches in holds a door, leads people clear or points the way, then expects a thank-you.
EXAMPLE BEAT: Mount Lady lands on a suspect a moment after Kamui Woods' branches close around him, waves to the phones, and tells the officer the capture is hers.
Below the Billboard.askTheNarratorPrompt:
I'm the Narrator. The night shift has just started, and the police radio never really goes quiet.

Ask me anything:
• "What's on the board tonight?" — calls, complaints and open cases your character knows about
• "Who works this neighborhood?" — the pros, officers and regulars on these streets
• "Is this legal?" — what Quirk law says about what you're about to do
• "Who needs help?" — who's hurt, who's missing and what stands in the way
• "What will the agency say?" — reports, pay, rankings and who takes the credit
• "Who saw that?" — witnesses, cameras and phones

Small cases still save lives. I answer from what your character could know or observe. You can also ask:
• "Who are the regulars?" — the shopkeepers, officers and neighbors your character knows by name
• "What's the pattern?" — the cases on this beat that look connected, as far as your character has seen
• "Who's on shift with me?" — partners and backup your character can call
